note: Our own writing about the courses, keyed by the name on the card. Used in preference to GSPro's description, which for most courses is a sentence of club marketing or nothing at all. Facts here are about the real place, not the sim build. Written 21 Oct 2026; every architect, year, tournament and hole detail was checked against a source at the time of writing. Three courses are deliberately absent because their facts could not be verified - see MISSING below.

descriptions.Augusta National: Perry Maxwell moved the tenth green in 1937, five years after Bobby Jones and Alister MacKenzie built the course, and it is still described as the hardest hole in Masters history. Gene Sarazen's double eagle at the fifteenth in 1935 is marked by the Sarazen Bridge in front of that green, and the loblolly pine on the seventeenth that Eisenhower wanted cut down stood until 2014. Marion Hollins assisted MacKenzie on the original design. Every hole carries the name of a plant, Tea Olive first, Holly last. Most people will only ever see it in a simulator.
descriptions.TPC Sawgrass: Pete and Alice Dye built it for the PGA Tour and it opened in the autumn of 1980; the Players Championship has been held there every year since 1982, having been played at Sawgrass Country Club next door before that. The seventeenth measures 137 yards, with a green roughly 78 feet long and one small bunker at the front, and that is the whole hole. Tiger Woods won the 1994 US Amateur here, beating Trip Kuehne in the final. The Dyes also laid out the resort's Valley course, with Bobby Weed and Jerry Pate.
descriptions.Pebble Beach: Jack Neville and Douglas Grant, 1919, laid out by two amateurs who routed it along the cliffs of Carmel Bay and left the interior holes to fend for themselves. The stretch from the sixth to the tenth sits directly above the Pacific, and the seventh — barely a hundred yards downhill to a green on a rock — is the most photographed short hole in golf. Six US Opens. The only one of the world's great courses anyone can book by phone.
descriptions.Royal Portrush (Dunluce): Harry Colt laid out the Dunluce links for a club founded in 1888 as the County Club, and his name is on the sixth hole, a 194-yard par 3. Calamity Corner, the sixteenth, is a par 3 of 236 yards. The seventh and eighth were built new for 2019 on ground taken from the club's Valley links, and the second was lengthened by forty yards at the same time. Other holes are named for Fred Daly and Darren Clarke. The Irish Open was played here as early as 1930.
descriptions.Carnoustie: The hardest of the Open rota, and it does not look it: flat Angus farmland with no dunes to speak of and nothing picturesque about it. The difficulty is in the wind, the bunkering, and the Barry Burn, which crosses the eighteenth fairway twice and finished Jean van de Velde in 1999 when he stood in it with his trousers rolled up. The closing three holes are the hardest finish in championship golf.
descriptions.Royal Troon: George Strath and Willie Fernie laid out the eighteen in 1888 and James Braid rebuilt it in 1923, the year of the first Open there; Martin Ebert revised it again in 2014. The eighth is the shortest hole in Open Championship golf at 123 yards, to a green of roughly 2,635 square feet. The eleventh, the Railway, has a blind tee shot over gorse, out of bounds along the line on the right, and a green that falls away. The sixth was the longest hole in Open history until 2023.
descriptions.Royal St George's: Laidlaw Purves laid it out in 1887, the year the club was formed, and Martin Ebert reworked it in 2016. Fifteen Opens have been played at Sandwich, from 1894 to 2021. The fourth, a 496-yard par 4, holds what is generally reckoned the deepest bunker in championship golf. Blind and half-blind shots are the normal condition rather than an oddity. The club has also run its own Challenge Cup over 36 holes every year since 1888 apart from the war years, and the Halford Hewitt has opened here since 1950.
descriptions.Royal Birkdale: The club began in 1889 and moved to its present ground in 1894, but the routing is the work of Frederick Hawtree and J.H. Taylor. Martin Hawtree rebuilt all eighteen greens in 1993, after the 1991 Open, and Tom Mackenzie made further changes before 2026, removing the old fourteenth and building a new par 3 under the clubhouse. The art deco clubhouse dates from 1935. Ten Opens so far with an eleventh in 2026, six Women's Opens, Ryder Cups in 1965 and 1969, and a Walker Cup in 1951.
descriptions.Royal Liverpool: Founded in 1869 on the racecourse of the Liverpool Hunt Club, with the first holes laid out by Robert Chambers and George Morris, younger brother of Old Tom; it reached eighteen holes in 1871 and Harry Colt rebuilt it early in the next century. Thirteen Opens have been played at Hoylake, the first in 1897, and in 2023 a short new par 3 of 136 yards played as the seventeenth. The Amateur Championship has been held here eighteen times since 1885, with another due in 2026.
descriptions.Turnberry: A public course in Pickerington, east of Columbus, and not the Ailsa links on the Ayrshire coast that shares its name. The confusion is the catalogue's fault rather than the builder's: the par sequence and the 6,775-yard black card match the Ohio course hole for hole, while Turnberry in Scotland is par 71 at 7,448 yards and has held four Opens. This one is a well-liked daily-fee eighteen with water on the back nine. Worth knowing before somebody tees up expecting the ninth hole along the rocks.
descriptions.Oakmont: Henry Fownes opened it in 1903 and never designed another course. There are 168 bunkers, and the Church Pews between the third and fourth fairways runs about 100 yards by 40 with thirteen grass ridges across it. The club's rakes had wider tines than normal, to furrow the sand; they were last used at the 1962 US Open and retired in 1964. Ten US Opens, more than any other course, plus three PGA Championships and six US Amateurs. Gil Hanse and Jim Wagner restored it across 2023 and 2024.
descriptions.Pinehurst No. 2: Donald Ross opened it in 1907 and kept adjusting it until he died in 1948. A 1974 redesign planted thick Bermuda rough across the whole course, which stayed until Bill Coore and Ben Crenshaw took all of it out and reshaped the fairways and bunkers, a restoration finished in 2011 for about $2.5 million. In 2014 the course held the US Open and the US Women's Open in consecutive weeks, won by Martin Kaymer and Michelle Wie. A statue of Payne Stewart stands by the eighteenth green.
descriptions.Shinnecock Hills: The club was founded in 1891 and is generally held to be the oldest incorporated golf club in the United States; it was one of five that formed the USGA in 1894, and its 1892 clubhouse, by Stanford White, is usually called the first purpose-built clubhouse in America. The course itself is William Flynn's, a complete new routing opened in 1931 after a highway extension threatened the old one. The seventh is a Redan copied from North Berwick, its green falling from front right to back left. Coore and Crenshaw restored Flynn's lines in the 2010s.
descriptions.Winged Foot (West): A.W. Tillinghast built both courses for a club founded in 1921, the West opening in 1923. For USGA championships the ninth is converted from a par 5 into a 514-yard par 4, among the longest in major championship history, while the twelfth stays a par 5 at 640 yards and is the sixth longest hole ever used in a major. Six US Opens have been played here, from 1929 to 2020, along with the 1997 PGA Championship. Gil Hanse and Jim Wagner renovated the West in 2018.
descriptions.Bethpage Black: Opened in 1936 and credited to Joseph Burbeck, the state park's superintendent, with A.W. Tillinghast consulting; who deserves the larger share is still argued over. The sign behind the first tee went up in the 1960s and reads that the course is extremely difficult and recommended only for highly skilled golfers. At the 2002 US Open, Tiger Woods was the only player in the field to finish under par. Rees Jones renovated it in 2015, and the 2033 PGA Championship is already booked.
descriptions.Merion (East): Hugh Wilson laid out the East and it opened in September 1912. The baskets on the pinheads are fourteen inches tall on solid metal poles, seven feet six inches overall, red on the front nine and orange on the back; they have been in use since at least 1916, and the 1950 US Open is the only USGA championship here played with flags instead. A plaque in the eighteenth fairway marks where Ben Hogan hit the 1-iron that got him into the playoff he won that year. Hanse and Wagner renovated it in 2014.
descriptions.The Olympic Club: Sam Whiting and Willie Watson built the Lake course in 1924 and Whiting rebuilt it three years later; Robert Trent Jones toughened it in 1953 for the championship that followed. Jack Fleck beat Ben Hogan over eighteen holes in 1955, Billy Casper beat Arnold Palmer in another playoff in 1966, and Scott Simpson and Lee Janzen later took titles off Tom Watson and Payne Stewart. The eighteenth green has been flattened and partly re-sloped; in 1998 a pin cut on a ridge sent putts rolling well past the hole.
descriptions.Oakland Hills (South): Donald Ross's South course formally opened in July 1918. Its reputation was made in 1951, when the club was allowed to tighten the setup to the point that only two sub-par rounds were shot all week; Ben Hogan's closing 67 was one of them, and afterwards the USGA stopped letting host clubs control the layout for a US Open. Chen Tze-chung made a double eagle at the second in the 1985 Open and then a quadruple bogey at the fifth on Sunday, hitting the ball twice with one swing. Gil Hanse rebuilt the course between 2019 and 2021.
descriptions.Oak Hill (East): Donald Ross built the East after the club moved out to Pittsford in 1921. Allen Creek acts as a lateral hazard on eight of the eighteen holes. Robert Trent Jones altered it in the early 1960s and Tom Fazio again before the 1989 US Open and the 2003 PGA; Andrew Green then pulled it back towards Ross in a restoration finished in 2019. Jack Nicklaus won the 1980 PGA here by seven shots, Curtis Strange the 1989 US Open by one, and Europe the 1995 Ryder Cup by a single point.
descriptions.Valhalla: Jack Nicklaus designed it for Dwight Gahm, a Louisville businessman who had the idea in 1981 and three sons to help him; it opened in 1986. The 2000 PGA Championship was the first decided under the three-hole aggregate playoff, Tiger Woods beating Bob May by a stroke. Mark Brooks had won the 1996 title at the first extra hole, with a birdie at the eighteenth. Xander Schauffele and Shane Lowry share the course record of 62, both set during the 2024 championship. The Solheim Cup arrives in 2028.
descriptions.Whistling Straits: Pete Dye built this on two miles of Lake Michigan shoreline in 1998, on what had been a flat army airfield. Everything you see was moved there: the dunes, the fescue, and something close to a thousand bunkers, many of them small enough to be decorative and all of them, officially, in play. That detail cost Dustin Johnson the 2010 PGA Championship when he grounded his club in one on the last and never knew it was a bunker at all. Three PGA Championships and the 2021 Ryder Cup.
descriptions.Kiawah Ocean Course: Pete and Alice Dye built it in time for the 1991 Ryder Cup, and Hurricane Hugo wrecked the site's dune ridge while construction was under way. The course was meant to sit behind those dunes; Alice Dye's suggestion was to raise the whole thing so every hole looked out over the water, which also left all eighteen exposed to the sea breeze. The resort counts ten holes along the Atlantic and eight running parallel behind them. Two PGA Championships, in 2012 and 2021, and the Senior PGA in 2007.
descriptions.Royal County Down: Newcastle, County Down, with the Mountains of Mourne behind the clubhouse and the Irish Sea down one side. Old Tom Morris was paid four pounds for the original layout in 1889. It is the most beautiful links in the world and one of the most unfair: blind tee shots over marram-topped dunes, bunkers with eyebrows of rough hanging over them, and gorse that takes a ball permanently. Rated first in the world more often than anywhere else.
descriptions.Royal Melbourne: Alister MacKenzie saw the site in 1926 and left again after a short visit; Alex Russell drew up the rest and built it with the head greenkeeper, Mick Morcom, and the West was ready for play in 1931. Russell then laid out the East in 1932. The sixth is the hole architects quote: a dogleg from a high tee with bunkers set at the corner, so the drive is a decision rather than a swing. Championships are played on a Composite course of East and West holes, as all three Presidents Cups were.
descriptions.Royal Dornoch: Old Tom Morris visited in 1886 and 1889 and is credited with most of the championship links. The present sixth to eleventh are George Duncan's, built after the Second World War on land bought to replace holes lost to a wartime airfield. Donald Ross grew up in the village, apprenticed with Morris at St Andrews, and was Dornoch's professional and keeper of the green from 1893 until he left for America in 1899. The club has held the Amateur Championship once, in 1985, and no modern professional tournament at all.
descriptions.Muirfield Village: Jack Nicklaus bought the land outside Columbus in 1966, began building six years later, and opened the club in May 1974. It has held the Ryder Cup in 1987, the Solheim Cup in 1998, the Presidents Cup in 2013 and the US Amateur in 1992. Nicklaus has kept revising his own course: the eighteenth was lengthened by forty yards in 2013 and its stream rerouted, bunkers were added at the tenth and seventeenth, and the fifth and fifteenth were the holes most altered in the work done after the 2020 Memorial.
descriptions.Riviera Country Club: George Thomas and William Bell opened it in 1926 as the Los Angeles Athletic Club's course. The tenth is a drivable par 4 of 315 yards ringed with bunkers, where position matters more than length. Hogan is said to have called the fourth the best par 3 in America, and he won the 1948 US Open here. Two PGA Championships, in 1983 and 1995, and the Los Angeles Open almost every year since 1973. Golf at the 2028 Olympics is scheduled for Riviera, and the US Open returns in 2031.
descriptions.Quail Hollow Club: George Cobb opened it on 3 June 1961; Arnold Palmer altered several holes in 1986 and Tom Fazio reworked it in 1997, 2003 and again between 2014 and 2016. The sixteenth green was moved eighty yards left in 2013 and now sits on the edge of the lake. Over four rounds of the 2017 PGA Championship the field played the last three holes a combined 488 over par. The Presidents Cup came in 2022, and Rory McIlroy's 61 from 2015 is still the course record.
descriptions.East Lake Golf Club: Tom Bendelow made the first layout for the Atlanta Athletic Club and Donald Ross redesigned it in 1913, giving each nine a finish at the clubhouse. Bobby Jones learned the game here and is said to have played his first and last rounds on it; his father ran the club for five years and Jones himself was president in 1946 and 1947. Rees Jones restored the Ross plan in the mid-1990s and Andrew Green worked on it again in 2023. The 1963 Ryder Cup was played here with Palmer as playing captain.
descriptions.Bay Hill Club: Dick Wilson laid out the first eighteen in 1961 and Bob Simmons built them; Simmons added the third nine, the Charger, after Wilson's death. Arnold Palmer bought the club in 1974 and owned it until he died in 2016, and it belongs now to his daughter and son-in-law, Amy and Roy Saunders. The tournament he founded has been played there every March since 1979. Wilson left far fewer courses than Ross or Tillinghast, and this one is usually named among his best.
descriptions.Harbour Town Golf Links: Pete Dye built it in 1967 with help from Jack Nicklaus. The greens average about 3,700 square feet against a tour average of 6,600, which is why the course still holds up at a little over 7,000 yards; overhanging trees can block a player out of the fairway on ten of the eighteen holes. Arnold Palmer won the first Heritage over Thanksgiving weekend in 1969 for $20,000. Webb Simpson's 262 in 2020 is the tournament record. The winner gets a tartan plaid jacket.
descriptions.TPC Scottsdale (Stadium): Weiskopf and Morrish, 1986, built in the desert north of Phoenix with spectators in mind before anyone else was doing it. The 16th is the result: a 160-yard par 3 enclosed on all sides by grandstands holding twenty thousand people who drink all day and boo anything short. Nowhere else in golf sounds like it. The rest is a fair, wide desert course that would be unremarkable without the week in February that makes it famous.
descriptions.Torrey Pines (South): William Francis Bell laid out both courses on the old Camp Callan army site above the cliffs, and the municipal complex opened in 1957; Rees Jones rebuilt the South in 2001 to make it fit for a US Open. It took seven years to arrive. The 2008 championship went to a Monday playoff, then to sudden death, and was settled on the ninety-first hole, the par-4 seventh, where Rocco Mediate bogeyed and Tiger Woods made par. It was the last US Open decided over eighteen extra holes.
descriptions.Colonial Country Club: Marvin Leonard built it in 1936 to settle an argument. He wanted to prove bentgrass greens would survive a Texas summer, and bought flat ground by the Trinity River to try it. He asked both John Bredemus and Perry Maxwell for plans, took parts of each, and the course is credited to the two of them. The third, fourth and fifth bend round the river through tall timber and are known as the Horrible Horseshoe. Hogan was a member, and said a straight ball got him into more trouble here than anywhere he knew.
descriptions.Firestone Country Club: Bert Way opened the South course on 10 August 1929, and Robert Trent Jones rebuilt it in 1960 for that year's PGA Championship. Arnold Palmer made a triple bogey at the sixteenth that week and called the course a monster; the hole is one of the longest par 5s anywhere, with a pond short of the green. Gary Player birdied the same hole late to win the 1972 PGA. The sixth is generally reckoned the hardest on the card, and the fifteenth hides a bunker left of the green.
descriptions.Innisbrook (Copperhead): Larry Packard opened it in 1974, one of four courses he laid out at the resort, and a 2015 restoration rebuilt the greens to USGA specification while keeping his shapes. The closing three are named Moccasin, Rattler and Copperhead, with a bronze snake at the sixteenth tee. The sixteenth is a long par 4 that the field bogeys about a third of the time, the seventeenth a par 3 with four bunkers round it, the eighteenth uphill. Padraig Harrington holds the course record at 61, set in 2012.
descriptions.Chambers Bay: Robert Trent Jones Jr. built it inside a working sand and gravel mine that Pierce County had bought in 1992, which meant fewer planning restrictions than usual; 1.4 million cubic yards of sand and dirt came out, were cleaned off site, and went back as shaping. It opened in June 2007. The single tree is a Douglas fir behind the fifteenth green, which is why that 246-yard par 3 is called Lone Fir. For the 2010 US Amateur the course was set at 7,742 yards, then the longest in USGA history.
descriptions.The Country Club (Brookline): The club was formed in January 1882 for riding and other outdoor pursuits; golf did not arrive until 1893, when three members laid out six holes, and Willie Campbell took it to nine the next summer and eighteen by 1899. William Flynn added the nine-hole Primrose course in 1927, and championships are played on a composite layout that borrows Primrose holes to replace three on the main course. Justin Leonard's forty-five-footer in 1999 and Ouimet's clinching putt in 1913 were on the same green, the seventeenth.
descriptions.Le Golf National: Hubert Chesneau and Robert von Hagge designed the Albatros with Pierre Thevenin; building started in July 1987 and the course opened on 5 October 1990. The French Open has been played there every year since 1991 apart from 1999 and 2001, which makes it one of the most heavily tested layouts in Europe. Europe won the 2018 Ryder Cup on it by 17.5 to 10.5. At the 2024 Olympics Scottie Scheffler took the men's gold at 19 under and Lydia Ko the women's at 10 under.
descriptions.Real Club Valderrama: Robert Trent Jones built it in the mid-1970s as Sotogrande New. It became Las Aves in 1981, and in 1984 Jaime Ortiz-Patino bought it, brought Jones back to redesign and extend, and renamed it Valderrama. The fourth, La Cascada, is the hole the club puts forward: a par 5 with a pond to the right of a two-tiered green. The Volvo Masters closed the European season here from 1988 to 1996 and again from 2002 to 2008, and the 1997 Ryder Cup was the first held in continental Europe.
descriptions.Wentworth (West): Harry Colt opened the West in 1926 on Surrey heath and sand. Ernie Els spent the winter of 2005-06 adding 310 yards and thirty bunkers, and kept revising the course for another decade. The seventeenth is the longest hole at 610 yards, the second the shortest at 154. The 1953 Ryder Cup was played here, the World Match Play ran at Wentworth from 1964 to 2007, and the BMW PGA Championship has been held on the West every year since 1984.
descriptions.Adare Manor: A Robert Trent Jones Sr course from the 1990s that J.P. McManus had Tom Fazio take apart and rebuild in 2016, down to every blade of grass. The result is immaculate rather than rugged, laid along the River Maigue in County Limerick with the manor house behind. It hosts the 2027 Ryder Cup, which is why the renovation happened. Parkland golf in a country better known for its links.
descriptions.Seminole: Donald Ross laid it out in 1929 for Edward Hutton, the investment banker. Dick Wilson restored it in 1957 after wartime neglect, and Coore and Crenshaw spent three years from 2016 rebuilding more than a hundred bunkers. All but four holes, the first, eighth, ninth and tenth, run against the dune ridges that frame the property. Nothing was televised from the club until a charity skins game in May 2020, and the Walker Cup followed in 2021. Most people will only ever see it in a simulator.
descriptions.Spyglass Hill: Robert Trent Jones Sr. opened it on 11 March 1966 after six years of planning and building; it was called Pebble Beach Pines until Samuel Morse renamed it. Every hole takes its name from Treasure Island, among them Blind Pew, Israel Hands and Long John Silver. The first, Treasure Island, is a downhill 597-yard par 5 that doglegs almost ninety degrees left. Jones called the fourth, Blind Pew, 376 yards with its green ringed in ice plant, his favourite par 4. The course record of 62 has been shot twice.
descriptions.Sahalee Country Club: Ted Robinson built the three nines over two years and the club opened in 1969 on a forested plateau; the name means high heavenly ground in Chinook. Fairways are cut through Douglas fir and red cedar, each hole averages five or six hazards, and every nine has two ponds in play. Rees Jones rebuilt the South and North nines in 1996 and the East nine after the 1998 PGA Championship, which Vijay Singh won. The Women's PGA has been held here twice, in 2016 and 2024.
descriptions.Torrey Pines (North): The other half of William Francis Bell's municipal pair above the La Jolla cliffs, opened in 1957 on ground that had been the Camp Callan army base. It plays to par 72 at 7,221 yards with a course rating of 75.8 and a slope of 134, against 78.8 and 148 for the South, which is the clearest measure of the gap between them. The San Diego tour stop uses both courses for the first two rounds and then the South alone for the weekend.
descriptions.Pine Needles: Donald Ross opened it in 1928. Peggy Kirk Bell, a charter member of the LPGA, bought the course with her husband and partners in 1953 and built a resort around it; she taught there for the rest of her life and is largely credited with bringing the US Women's Open to Southern Pines. John Fought restored the greens and bunkers from old aerial photographs in 2004. The Women's Opens went to Annika Sorenstam in 1996, Karrie Webb in 2001, Cristie Kerr in 2007 and Minjee Lee in 2022.
descriptions.Waialae Country Club: Seth Raynor laid out the course for a club founded in 1927. The event now called the Sony Open began in 1965 as the Hawaiian Open and opens the PGA Tour's calendar year in January, the first full-field tournament of the season. The ground is flat and the palms block little, so the defence is wind off the Pacific and small targets rather than length. For a Raynor course it is a long way from the north-east, where almost all his others sit.
descriptions.Hamilton G&CC: Harry Colt laid out eighteen holes at Ancaster in 1914, now the West and South nines; Robbie Robinson added a third nine, the East, in 1974. Martin Ebert directed an eleven-million-dollar restoration of all twenty-seven from 2019, the first eighteen reopening in 2021 and the East nine in the summer of 2022. Seven Canadian Opens have been played here, from J. Douglas Edgar's win in 1919 and Tommy Armour's in 1930 through to Rory McIlroy in 2019 and Robert MacIntyre in 2024.
descriptions.Memorial Park: The park was laid out by Hare and Hare in 1924 and John Bredemus rebuilt the golf course, which reopened in 1936. Tom Doak dug up all eighteen holes from January 2019, with Brooks Koepka as player consultant; Koepka pushed for a fifth par 3 and for keeping them all under 200 yards, and the bunker count came down from 54 to 19. It reopened that November and the Houston Open moved there in 2020. The Memorial Park Conservancy has run the course since 2016.
descriptions.Blue Monster at Doral: Dick Wilson opened it in 1962, and the Doral Open ran on it without a break until 2006, then the WGC-Cadillac from 2007 until that event was moved to Mexico City after 2016. Gil Hanse and Jim Wagner modernised the course in 2014. Stephen Ames holds the record at 61, set in 2000. LIV Golf has played its Miami event here since 2022, and a PGA Tour signature event is due back in 2026.
descriptions.Butler National: George Fazio designed it in 1972 on the old York Country Club land, with his nephew Tom supervising the build; it was cleared and seeded inside two years. The Western Open was played there from 1974 to 1990 and then left, because the club does not admit women members, and no PGA Tour or USGA event has been held there since. Roughly forty bunkers, more dogleg lefts than rights, and flat tree-lined ground that gives nothing away.
descriptions.Pelican Golf Club: Donald Ross finished the original course in 1925, four years before Seminole, and it spent decades as the Belleview Biltmore layout, remodelled more than once. The Doyle family bought it in 2017 and brought in Beau Welling, who found too little record of Ross's work to attempt a restoration and instead rebuilt it in the manner of the period, widening fairways and reworking greens and bunkers. The LPGA has played there since 2020, now as the ANNIKA driven by Gainbridge.
descriptions.Ritz-Carlton Grande Lakes: Greg Norman's design, opened with the resort in 2003, with Matthew Dusenberry credited alongside him. It runs to 7,122 yards at par 72, and the routing was drawn to leave the wetlands and their wildlife where they were, which earned it certification as an Audubon Cooperative Sanctuary. It belongs to a hotel rather than a club, so unlike most Florida courses of this standard it can simply be booked for a morning.
descriptions.RTJ Grand National (Lake): One of three courses at Opelika on the Robert Trent Jones Trail, the chain of public courses built across Alabama in the early 1990s. Twelve of the Lake Course's holes run along the shore of the 600-acre Lake Saugahatchee, part of the thirty-two of Grand National's fifty-four that the Trail counts along the water. Jones is said to have called the site the best he had ever seen for a golf complex. The 2015 Barbasol Championship here was the first PGA Tour event in Alabama since the 1990 PGA Championship.
descriptions.Sea Island (Seaside): Walter Travis laid out the first nine in the 1920s, and Harry Colt and Charles Alison built a back nine and reworked Travis's holes in 1929. What is played now is Tom Fazio's 1999 reworking, which joined the Colt and Alison nine to nine holes of the resort's old Marshside course. Davis Love III, whose home course it is, worked with Fazio and hosts the RSM Classic, played there since 2010. Marsh, Atlantic wind and raised greens do the defending.
descriptions.Silverado (North): The original eighteen opened in 1955 and became the North when Robert Trent Jones Jr. redesigned it in 1966 and added the South. Johnny Miller revised it in 2011, adding 250 yards, widening fairways, repositioning bunkers and rebuilding the tees. The Kaiser International was played here from 1968 to 1976 and the Anheuser-Busch Classic from 1977 to 1980; the tour came back in October 2014 and the event has changed sponsor and name three times since.
descriptions.The Dunes Club: Robert Trent Jones Sr. built it at the end of the 1940s, with sources split between 1948 and 1949 for the opening. The thirteenth, called Waterloo, is the hole that made its name: a par 5 of about 590 yards that bends most of the way round a lake, and Dan Jenkins once placed it among the eighteen best holes in America. Jones came back in 1976 to change five holes, and his son Rees has worked on the course since.
descriptions.TPC Southwind: Ron Prichard designed it with Hubert Green and Fuzzy Zoeller advising, and it opened in 1988; the Memphis tour stop moved over from Colonial in Cordova the following year. There are ninety-four bunkers as well as the water. The fourteenth, at 239 yards, is one of the hardest par 3s the tour plays, and Bob Estes made the only hole-in-one there in competition, in 2002. In 2011 the course was ranked ninth hardest of the fifty-one the tour used.
descriptions.Druids Glen: Pat Ruddy and Tom Craddock laid it out and it opened in 1995. The Irish Open was played there for its first four years, 1996 to 1999, Sergio Garcia closing with a 64 to win the last of them, and the Seve Trophy followed in 2002. The twelfth, Heartbreak Hill, is a 171-yard par 3 to a heavily bunkered green above a steep fall. The club's own nickname for the place is the Augusta of Europe, which is not a claim everyone accepts.
descriptions.Prestwick Golf Club (Tournament): The Open Championship started here in 1860 and stayed for the first twelve, which makes this the oldest championship venue in golf. Old Tom Morris laid it out over twelve holes on a strip of Ayrshire duneland. It still plays like something from before the rules settled down: blind drives over the Cardinal bunker at the third, the Himalayas at the fifth played entirely over a dune with nothing to aim at, and a closing stretch that modern design would never permit. Not a test of golf so much as a reminder of where it came from.
descriptions.Cypress Point: Alister MacKenzie's 1928 course on the Monterey Peninsula, and the one architects name when asked for the best. It runs through pine, then dune, then out onto the rocks: the fifteenth and sixteenth sit on the Pacific, the sixteenth a 230-yard par 3 played across an inlet of open ocean with no bail-out worth the name. Barely more than two hundred members. Most people will only ever see it in a simulator.
descriptions.National Golf Links of America: Charles Blair Macdonald put the idea forward in 1904: an American course whose holes answered the famous holes of Britain, because he thought nothing built in the United States had tried. Work started around 1907, and a local surveyor named Seth Raynor ran the construction and learned a trade from it that he would take across the country. The 13th copies the 11th at St Andrews, the 15th is a Redan after North Berwick, and the 14th, Cape, was Macdonald's own. It held the first Walker Cup in 1922.
descriptions.Sand Hills: Dick Youngscap was told that to get the dunes he wanted he would have to buy all 8,000 acres, so he bought them. Coore and Crenshaw first walked the site in September 1990 and took until the spring of 1993 over the routing, finding well over a hundred possible holes before settling on eighteen; a land swap with the neighbour made the 12th through 15th possible. Construction moved under 4,000 cubic yards of earth. It opened in 1995 and changed what architects thought they were allowed to leave alone.
descriptions.Bandon Dunes: David McLay Kidd was 26 when Mike Keiser first walked him over the 1,200-odd acres he had bought for $2.4 million, roughly half the asking price. Much of the ground was forest, or buried under six to twelve feet of gorse. The course opened on 19 May 1999 and made Kidd's name at a stroke. The 16th, a par 4 across a steep ravine with its landing areas staggered by a sandy bank, sits so near the cliff that the site was briefly considered for the clubhouse before being kept for golf.
descriptions.Pacific Dunes: Tom Doak, 2001, the second course at Bandon and the one that made his name. It breaks the rules cheerfully — back-to-back par 3s on the back nine, four of them in total, an out-and-back routing that ignores the usual nine-and-nine — and gets away with it because every hole sits where the ground wanted one. Several run along the cliff edge a hundred feet above the Pacific. Walking only, like everything at Bandon.
descriptions.Old Macdonald: Tom Doak and Jim Urbina built it in homage to Charles Blair Macdonald and it opened in 2010. Doak has said the team began with about twenty favourite Macdonald holes and features and found room for sixteen or seventeen: a Redan, a Short, a Long, an Eden, nods to the Road Hole and to the Double Plateau green. Where the ground would not take a template they did not force one, so the back-to-back 14th and 15th are nobody's copy of anything. Keiser had originally wanted a replica of Lido.
descriptions.Bandon Trails: Coore and Crenshaw's 2005 course leaves the dunes for forest and comes back again. The hole that still causes arguments is the 14th, a short par 4 to a plateau green; Coore admitted they were pushing the envelope and offered to change it if the owner wanted it changed. Nobody did, though the landing area and green were later softened so that fewer shots were rejected. A driver can run through the back of the green, and laying up leaves an awkward wedge from the bottom of the valley.
descriptions.Sheep Ranch: Golf of a sort has been played on this ground since 2001, when it held thirteen greens and no settled routing. Coore and Crenshaw formalised it and the course opened on 1 June 2020 on what is reckoned the windiest site at the resort, which is part of the reason there is no sand: Coore argued that fescue would hold balls back from the cliffs better than bunkers that would simply blow out. The 3rd and 16th share a vast double green out on Five Mile Point, the furthest peninsula on the property.
descriptions.Streamsong Red: Mosaic, a fertiliser company, had mined the central Florida site for phosphate and left sand spoil heaped up to seventy-five feet, terrain no other Florida course has. There was room for only thirty-one holes on the good ground shared with Tom Doak's Blue, so Coore and Crenshaw laid the Red's first five across stripped-out land; both courses opened in 2012. The par-3 16th plays over Canyon Lake to a Biarritz green some seventy yards from front to back, sharing the water with the Blue's 7th.
descriptions.Streamsong Blue: Tom Doak's half of the original pair at Streamsong, opened alongside Coore and Crenshaw's Red in 2012 rather than last of the three: Gil Hanse's Black followed in 2017. The ground is the same worked-out phosphate mine, and Doak drew the higher sand. The 7th is the hole everyone photographs, a par 3 with the green set between Canyon Lake short of it and a wall of sand hills behind, pointed at the same water the Red's 16th has to cross.
descriptions.Streamsong Black: Gil Hanse and Jim Wagner opened the third course at Streamsong on 29 September 2017, the year after their Olympic course in Rio. The greens are the point, among the largest and most heavily contoured anywhere: the 9th is an elevated punchbowl, the 13th has two greens, and the par-3 17th finishes against an infinity edge. Five par 5s of widely different lengths make up the par of 73. Reviewers tend to call the putting surfaces fascinating and frustrating in the same sentence.
descriptions.Cabot Cliffs: The second course at Inverness, and the one that made the place internationally known. Coore and Crenshaw's 176-yard 16th is among the most photographed par 3s in golf: the shot crosses a chasm to a tear-drop green on the cliff edge, and Coore has said the wind and the day's flag decide nearly everything about how it is played. By his account the design question was simply whether the elevations and the available green site would support a hole there at all.
descriptions.Cape Kidnappers: Julian Robertson, the American financier who owned the station, commissioned Tom Doak in late 2001, and the course opened in the southern summer of 2004-05. The 15th, Pirate's Plank, is the hole that divides people: a par 5 of around 594 metres running out along a narrowing finger of ridge to a green at the cliff edge, with nothing worth the name either side. Tree growth had closed its sight lines by the time Doak returned for a regrassing marking twenty years; cut back, it reads as a plank again.
descriptions.Barnbougle Dunes: Richard Sattler was growing potatoes on the dunes outside Bridport when Mike Keiser, who had heard about the land, came to look and suggested what might be done with eighty hectares of it. Tom Doak and Mike Clayton laid out two returning nines in the old out-and-back manner and the course opened in 2004, the reason there is a resort on that coast at all. The 7th, a short par 3, is known as Tom's Little Devil.
descriptions.Teeth of the Dog: Pete Dye spent three years living on site in the Dominican Republic before this opened in 1971, and seven of its holes run directly along the Caribbean with the water in play on every one. Dye's own line was that he created eleven holes and God created seven. Still the best course in the Caribbean by common consent, and the one that turned Casa de Campo into a resort worth flying to.
descriptions.Kapalua Plantation: Coore and Crenshaw's 1991 course on the hillside above Kapalua was, by one account, routed backwards from its finish: the architects found the closing hole first and built the rest around it. The 18th runs 663 yards downhill and usually downwind with jungle canyon down the left, and it is the reason the field that opens the PGA Tour season here each January arrives thinking about eagles rather than pars. Past winners there include Tiger Woods, Dustin Johnson and Ernie Els.
descriptions.Tobacco Road: Mike Strantz built it in a worked-out sand quarry in the North Carolina sandhills, on ground that grew tobacco before it was mined, and it opened in 1998. He had come up through Tom Fazio's construction crews before setting up on his own at the end of the 1980s. The blindness is mostly a bluff: where the shot cannot be seen the fairway is often a hundred yards wide and the greens feed towards the hole. The closing hole plays out of the quarry to a landing area nobody can see.
descriptions.The Grove XXIII: Bobby Weed built it on a flat former citrus grove on the edge of Hobe Sound, and it opened in the autumn of 2019 with no announcement at all; word only got round the following year. The name is the owner's number in Roman numerals. Membership runs to fewer than a hundred, and local reporting put the cost of the project at about twenty million dollars. Almost nobody outside that membership has walked it.
descriptions.Trump Aberdeen (Old): Martin Hawtree's 2012 course on the Menie Estate, about twelve miles north of Aberdeen, runs roughly three miles along the coast and measures 7,428 yards from the back. The dunes were written about in golf magazines years before anything was built on them, and the development was fought over for just as long. A second layout, the New Course, followed in 2025, and the DP World Tour scheduled its Scottish Championship here from that year.
descriptions.Black Desert Resort: Tom Weiskopf's last design, with Phil Smith, laid through the black lava flows at Ivins under the red rock of southern Utah. Weiskopf died in August 2022, before it opened for play on 27 May 2023, but had already recorded a hole-by-hole flyover narration setting out what he intended. Two short par 4s, the 5th and the 14th, are meant to be drivable. The PGA Tour arrived in 2024 with the Black Desert Championship, which has since taken a new sponsor's name.
descriptions.The Ledges: Michael Hurdzan and Dana Fry's 2000 course sits on the bluff above Huntsville, the clubhouse at 1,582 feet, the highest point in the city, with the Tennessee valley below. Golf Magazine named Hurdzan its designer of the year in 2003 largely on the strength of this work. Fry's later firm has since laid out a short-game academy at the club, with a 5,500 square foot putting green and a separate chipping green.
descriptions.Trump National Doral (Golden Palm): One of five eighteens at the Doral resort in Miami, and one of two remade by Gil Hanse's team after the resort changed hands in 2011 and roughly fifty million dollars went into the golf. Jim Wagner ran the work on site and the course reopened in September 2015; he said at the time it would be second only to the Blue Monster for difficulty, and at least one reviewer since has found it harder than the Blue Monster. Credit for the original layout is disputed in the record.
descriptions.Trump National Doral (Red Tiger): The shortest of the Doral courses and the first of the resort's others to be remade by Gil Hanse's team: Jim Wagner reopened it in February 2015, describing it as deliberately intimate and aimed at the average player. Water was brought into play on fourteen holes, the bunkering was reworked, and the real defence was left in the green complexes. It was unveiled alongside the Blue Monster in the early 1960s, though the scorecard has never settled whose design it originally was.
descriptions.Trump National Doral (Silver Fox): The quietest of the Doral courses and the one with the thinnest paper trail. It carried the instructor Jim McLean's name for years before being renamed; course directories trace the layout to a Bruce Devlin and Robert von Hagge design from the mid-1980s, altered by Jerry Pate and then redesigned by McLean in 2008. The 14th has an island green. All of it sits behind the Blue Monster, which Dick Wilson opened in 1962 and which held the Doral Open until 2006.
descriptions.Chicago Golf Club: The club moved out to Wheaton in the mid-1890s, onto 200 acres of the Patrick farm bought for $28,000, and Macdonald routed both nines clockwise because he fought the ball left to right. The U.S. Open came in 1897, 1900 and 1911. By 1917 Macdonald had turned on his own work, calling it one of the worst courses in the country compared with its former standing, and Seth Raynor rebuilt it: nine new holes opened in July 1922 and the rest a year later. What is played now is substantially Raynor's.
descriptions.Marshfield Country Club: Not a Donald Ross course, whatever is often said of it. The architect was Wayne Stiles, the New England designer whose work around Boston has only lately been properly credited. The first nine dates to the early 1920s, with the club's own account putting the first golf shot struck in Marshfield on 4 July 1923, and Stiles added the second nine in 1931. It went public in 1965 and a further nine was built in 1974. Par 70 over 6,392 yards on the South Shore.
descriptions.Monte Rei: Jack Nicklaus's North Course opened in 2007 in the eastern Algarve, inland from the coast near Tavira, and Top 100 Golf Courses rates it first in the region. Water is in play on eleven of the holes. A second Nicklaus course has been planned on the estate for years without being built, and the North is due to shut for several months of 2026 for major work. Much of the best-in-Portugal talk originates with the resort itself.
descriptions.Pinehurst No. 8: Tom Fazio's course for the resort's hundredth year, opened in 1996 on the old gun club land away from the main cluster of courses. The wetlands there gave him water to work with, which the sandhills courses do not have: the 14th asks how much of a wetland to bite off from the tee. It is designated an Audubon Signature Sanctuary. A renovation in 2022 rebuilt greens, bunkers and drainage while leaving the architecture alone.
descriptions.Royal New Kent: Mike Strantz's Virginia course took Golf Digest's best new course award for 1997. Its later history is the interesting part: the owner closed it and nearby Stonehouse at the end of 2017, it lay dormant about six months, and a South Carolina operator bought it in June 2018 for $1.1 million, a fraction of the $5 million paid for it in 2001. Some $2 million went into new greens, Champion Bermuda in place of bent, and 105 rebuilt bunkers. It reopened on 29 March 2019.
descriptions.Rumbling Bald (Bald Mountain): George Cobb, who built the par-3 course at Augusta National, laid this out with his protege W.B. Lewis; sources date it to 1968 or the early 1970s. It has an unusual balance for a mountain course, five par 5s and five par 3s. The 16th green appears in Dirty Dancing, which was filmed around Lake Lure in 1987. The resort's other eighteen, Apple Valley, is a 1986 design by Dan Maples, son of Ellis Maples.
descriptions.Apes Hill: The course first opened in 2009, into the teeth of the recession, and then went years underused before Ron Kirby was brought in to rebuild it. The new layout opened in November 2022 at 7,002 yards, with forward tees at 5,034. Kirby, who had worked with Robert Trent Jones Sr and Jack Nicklaus and died the following year at ninety, cut the bunker count from 107 to 38 and reduced the sprinkler heads by more than half, which on an island short of water is not a cosmetic decision.
descriptions.Ballyowen: Roger Rulewich, for many years Robert Trent Jones Sr's lead design associate, laid it out, and it opened in June 1998 as the first of three courses he built for the Crystal Springs resort in the Jersey highlands. It covers about 250 acres with water on five holes, and Golfweek has ranked it second among the state's public courses. A piper plays outside the clubhouse pub in the evenings.
descriptions.Balsam Mountain Preserve: Arnold Palmer and Ed Seay's course, with Harrison Minchew also credited, opened in 2007 inside a private Blue Ridge development west of Sylva. It opened in pieces: ten holes for members at Memorial Day, the full eighteen on 1 September. The golf runs between roughly 3,200 and 3,700 feet, with high points closer to 4,000, while the wider preserve climbs a good deal higher. Par 70 over 6,754 yards, which for mountain golf counts as restraint.
descriptions.Barnbougle Lost Farm: Coore and Crenshaw's course opened in December 2010 next door to the Dunes, and it has twenty holes, all of them in play in a normal round: extra short par 3s sit beside the 13th and the 18th, numbered 13A and 18A. The ground runs between Bass Strait and the Forester River on land the Sattler family farmed, with the Tasmanian hinterland inland. Played as the full twenty it comes to a par of 78.
descriptions.Bluejack National: The first course Tiger Woods designed in the United States, on 755 acres north of Houston. There is no rough anywhere on it and the landing areas are wide. The club also has a ten-hole short course, The Playgrounds, which Woods helped lay out: when it opened on 2 March 2016 with Woods watching, an eleven-year-old from Corpus Christi holed the first shot ever struck there, on the 81-yard first hole.
descriptions.Branson Hills: Chuck Smith designed it with Bobby Clampett consulting, and it opened in 2009. The opening tee shot falls more than 130 feet to the fairway, which sets the terms for what the Ozark ridges do to the rest of the round. Six tee sets run from 7,324 yards down to 5,323. Golf Digest ranked it ninth in Missouri in 2011-12 and twelfth for 2025-26.
descriptions.Camberley Heath: Harry Colt's course opened in 1913, though one account puts the official opening on 1 January 1914. Colt left for America before the work was done, and a Mr F.G. Waterer finished the construction and altered several holes. The Duke of York, later George VI, was an honorary member, and the Prince of Wales followed him as patron. It has held the Lagonda Trophy and served as regional qualifying for the Open, and Frank Pont now advises the club on keeping Colt's features intact.
descriptions.Cape Wickham Links: Mike DeVries and Darius Oliver built it on the north-west corner of King Island, out in Bass Strait, and it opened in 2015. The lighthouse at the northern end dates from 1861, stands 48 metres, and is often the only thing to aim at; it is reckoned the tallest on any golf course anywhere. The closing hole doglegs right around Victoria Cove to a plateau green, with the beach itself doing the work of a bunker.
descriptions.Coeur d'Alene National Reserve: A Tom Weiskopf and Phil Smith course on the bluffs high above Lake Coeur d'Alene, which spent its earlier life as the Club at Rock Creek. The front nine is open and the back nine shut in by forest, with enough fall between holes to look down on the lake from a long way up. Golf Digest's panel had it first in Idaho from 2005 to 2009, second from 2011 to 2022 and fourth since. It grows bluegrass fairways, unlike neighbouring Black Rock.
descriptions.Corica Park South: A 1957 William F. Bell municipal in Alameda, reopened in the summer of 2018 after Rees Jones and Greenway Golf rebuilt it on the model of the Melbourne sandbelt: fast fairways, run-up ramps into low-slung greens, wispy fescue. Making it drain through a Bay Area winter meant moving more than a million cubic yards of fill to lift the site about eight feet, and a wet winter cost the project five months. Golf.com named it the best municipal renovation of that year.
descriptions.Dismal River (White): The White is the Jack Nicklaus course at Dismal River, opened in 2006; Tom Doak's Red followed in 2013. It runs 7,353 yards to a par of 72 through the Nebraska Sandhills, and it is routinely called one of the least Nicklaus-like courses Nicklaus has built, which on this ground is meant as a compliment. The club is private, though prospective members can apply for a single familiarisation round when the course is free.
descriptions.Dunstanburgh Castle: Golf has been played on this links since 1900, when nine holes were laid out below the ruins. Sir Arthur Munro Sutherland bought the estate in 1919 and brought in James Braid, who lengthened four holes, shortened four and added one; accounts date the work to 1920 or 1922. The course reached eighteen holes in stages, finishing in 1936, and remains close to what Braid left. The National Trust owns the ground, which is a Site of Special Scientific Interest.
descriptions.Farmlinks: Michael Hurdzan and Dana Fry had more or less free choice of the land, and the course opened in 2003, built by a fertiliser company as a working test plot that would also take real play. More than thirty grasses have been grown on it, among them a heat-tolerant bentgrass developed with Auburn University and called AU Victory. For years about a thousand superintendents and industry people came through annually on an all-expenses-paid visit. The family sold the fertiliser business in 2006; the golf stayed.
descriptions.Fishers Island Club: Seth Raynor's last course, finished in 1926 on an island off the Connecticut coast that you reach by ferry or not at all. It is a catalogue of the template holes Raynor and C.B. Macdonald borrowed from Britain — Redan, Biarritz, Punchbowl — laid across a peninsula with Long Island Sound on three sides. A tiny membership and a short season keep it unknown to most golfers and ranked in the world's top ten by everyone who has seen it.
descriptions.Geneva National (Palmer): Arnold Palmer and Ed Seay's course opened in 1991, the first of three at Geneva National, with a brief lakeside stretch along Lake Como at the 16th and 17th and woodland or housing for the rest. It plays 7,171 yards to a par of 72, rated 74.8 off the back with a slope of 140. Gary Player's course arrived in two halves in 1995 and 2000; Lee Trevino's dates from the same year as Palmer's.
descriptions.Gold Mountain Olympic: John Harbottle III laid out Bremerton's second eighteen, which opened in 1996 at a little over 7,000 yards. The two national championships are the 2006 U.S. Amateur Public Links and the 2011 U.S. Junior Amateur, which is a strong record for a course a city built, owns and still runs itself. Harbottle worked mostly in the Pacific Northwest, and often on public ground.
descriptions.Golf Club Davos: Golf has been played at Davos since the 1920s, and the club dates itself to 1929. The present layout is Donald Harradine's, extended to eighteen holes in the mid-1960s. It sits at around 1,500 metres in Davos-Dorf, which holds the season to roughly five months a year, and the ground is gentler than the setting implies: open parkland, mildly undulating, a little over 5,400 metres from the yellow tees.
descriptions.Golf Club of Tennessee: Bronson Ingram, Toby Wilt and George Gillett formed the club in 1988, and Tom Fazio's course opened for members in March 1991 across 317 acres of forest and rocky bluff west of Nashville. It was runner-up for Golf Digest's best new private course that year, and as of 2017 the same magazine had it 163rd among America's 200 greatest. It has stayed quiet, private, and largely unphotographed.
descriptions.Greywolf: Doug Carrick's 1999 course at Panorama, in the Purcells, was routed around a single hole: Carrick has said he would plan the whole course around the 6th, and that is effectively what he did. It crosses Hopeful Canyon to a green on the cliff, from tees at roughly 155, 175 and 200 yards. The Globe and Mail reckoned it the newcomer that would finally challenge Banff's Devil's Cauldron as the most talked-about par 3 in Canada.
descriptions.Itasca Country Club: The course dates from 1925 and is credited to James Foulis, who had won the second U.S. Open in 1896 and been Chicago Golf Club's first professional and greenkeeper, hired by Macdonald in 1895; he went on to lay out the first course in a good many Midwestern towns. Most of what is played at Itasca is still his, original greens included, with later work going mainly into irrigation, tees and cart paths. Robert Bruce Harris is credited with a redesign in 1986.
descriptions.Kearney Hills: Pete Dye and his son P.B. built it for the City of Lexington and it opened in 1989: mounds, moguls and grass bunkers over rumpled ground. The Senior PGA Tour played the Bank One Classic here for eight years from 1990, Gary Player winning twice. Tim Clark took the 1997 U.S. Amateur Public Links on it, and the women's edition came in 2007. The city's parks division still operates it.
descriptions.Kiawah Island (Cassique): Tom Watson built it on old farm fields along the tidal marshes of the Kiawah River and it opened in 2000. Five Open Championships went into it fairly literally: a burn after Turnberry, Spectacles bunkers after Carnoustie, a Hell Bunker borrowed from St Andrews. The front nine is open, the back runs into maritime forest. Golf Digest has it in the second hundred of its American ranking, as high as 85th in the past; Planet Golf considers it over-shaped and short of strategy.
descriptions.Ko'olau Golf Club: Dick Nugent built it below the Ko'olau range on the windward side of Oahu, with Jack Tuthill consulting, and it opened in 1992. The USGA gave it a slope of 162 from the back tees and in 1994 called it the toughest course in America; the figure has since come down to around 152. The 18th is a 476-yard par 4 with two forced carries over ravine, the second of them to the green, about 200 yards of it from the blue tees.
descriptions.Lahontan: Tom Weiskopf's 1998 course in the forest north of Lake Tahoe, private, and built on a pattern he used often: tee shots that look confined by trees into fairways that turn out to be generous. Water is in play on five holes, and the 2nd, nicknamed Gooseneck, is the one reviewers single out. It runs 7,335 yards to a par of 72, rated 75.0 with a slope of 146, and Golf Digest had it 30th in California for 2025-26.
descriptions.Le Diable: Michael Hurdzan and Dana Fry's course opened at Mont-Tremblant in 1998, three years after the resort's Le Geant. The sand is what people remember: the waste areas and bunkers are filled with red sand, and there is a great deal of it on the flatter front nine, where narrow fairways run between them. The back nine climbs into the mountain and trades sand for dense forest that swallows anything offline. It plays 7,056 yards from the black tees.
descriptions.Lethbridge Country Club: The members' early golf was on the river flood plain and then at the jail farm, before the move to the present ground in the 1920s. Stanley Thompson first came to Lethbridge in 1929, and in 1932 the Lethbridge Herald described the first nine holes of an eighteen-hole course laid out by him. The second nine did not arrive until 1983, and Les Furber redesigned the course in 2011, so not much of Thompson's hand is still legible. Golf Club Atlas argues the club is older than it claims, with a course open by 1912.
descriptions.Lew Wentz Memorial: A Perry Maxwell municipal in Ponca City, Oklahoma, from the 1930s, paid for by an oil man who gave most of his money away. Maxwell's greens are the reason it is worth knowing: the same restless contouring he brought to Prairie Dunes and to Augusta's back nine, on a course anyone could afford to play. One of the best public courses in the state and almost unknown outside it.
descriptions.Lofoten Links: The English architect Jeremy Turner built it with the owner, Frode Hov, growing it from six holes in 1998 into a full eighteen that opened on 4 July 2015. It sits on Gimsoy, one of the Lofoten islands. The 2nd is the hole it is known for: a par 3 of about 140 metres to a two-tiered green on a rock outcrop with sea on three sides and a single pot bunker guarding the front.
descriptions.Lofoten Links (Northern Lights): The same Gimsoy links, which at that latitude gets golf under the midnight sun through the summer and under aurora in the dark months. Turner has said the course is built over an old Viking burial ground, and two graves of that period lie within it; one is marked on the 1st, a drivable par 4 played across a cove. The eighteen-hole course was completed in 2015, having grown out of six holes laid out from 1998.
descriptions.Mammoth Dunes: David McLay Kidd's course at Sand Valley opened on 31 May 2018, twenty years after Mike Keiser first hired him at Bandon. It was the most argued-over opening of that year and took Golf Magazine's best new course award; Golf.com's architecture critic reckoned it the better of the two eighteens then at the resort, which was not the expected verdict. Par 73 over 6,935 yards of sand barrens in central Wisconsin.
descriptions.Manele Golf Course: Jack Nicklaus's 1993 course above Hulopoe Bay on Lanai, laid over lava outcrops, with three holes running along cliffs two hundred feet above the water. The 12th is a par 3 of about 202 yards played from one cliff to another; Bill and Melinda Gates were married on that tee in 1994, Gates having booked every hotel room and helicopter on the island to keep it private. The resort now lets the hole out for weddings, capped at about fifty guests.
descriptions.Ohoopee Match Club: Gil Hanse, 2018, built in the sandhills of south Georgia for one purpose: match play. There are no stroke-play tees in the usual sense and the card is close to irrelevant — you choose a line, your opponent chooses theirs, and the holes are wide enough that both can be right. Fast, firm, sandy ground that plays the way the Carolinas sandhills used to before irrigation. A private club with no tournament ambitions at all.
descriptions.Old Head Golf Links: John and Patrick O'Connor bought the 220-acre headland in 1989 and spent most of a decade getting a course onto it; it opened in 1997. Ron Kirby, who had worked for both Nicklaus and Player, finished the design, with Eddie Hackett, Paddy Merrigan, Liam Higgins and Joe Carr consulting and Haulie O'Shea doing the building. Forty-one routings were tried before one was settled on. Nine of the holes run along the cliff tops.
descriptions.Old Works: Construction began in 1994 on the Upper Works, where ore from Butte was smelted until the plant was abandoned. Waste rock heavy with copper and zinc was consolidated, contoured and capped with limestone and sixteen inches of soil, with drainage and water monitoring beneath; Atlantic Richfield spent around forty million dollars on the cleanup and the course together and then handed it to the town. It opened in May 1997, reported at the time as the first course built on an EPA Superfund site. Anaconda-Deer Lodge County owns it.
descriptions.Ozarks National: Missouri's only Coore and Crenshaw course, opened in the spring of 2019 after a preview season the previous autumn, and named Golf Digest's best new public course of that year. It plays 7,036 yards from the back. The 13th crosses a creek on a timber bridge four hundred feet long and sixty feet up, which is the sort of engineering the Ozark valleys force on an architect who has decided he wants a particular green site.
descriptions.Pacific Grove Golf Links: The first nine, through the forest, was laid out by H. Chandler Egan, a former U.S. Amateur champion, and opened on 9 May 1932; Samuel Morse of Pebble Beach is said to have sold the land to the local chamber of commerce for ten dollars on condition it stayed golf. Jack Neville added the dunes nine in 1960, and a new clubhouse went in between the two, which is why the round begins with two par 3s. The Point Pinos lighthouse, lit since 1855, stands on the property.
descriptions.Paradise Canyon: Bill Newis, an Alberta architect with sixty-odd courses to his name and most of them in the province, laid it out in the Oldman River valley at Lethbridge; the club dates it to 1992. It is a par 71 of about 6,810 yards, short by current standards, so the defence is the badland ground rather than the length: coulee walls, abrupt changes of level and a few hard climbs.
descriptions.Payne's Valley: Tiger Woods's first public-access design, opened in 2020 in the Missouri Ozarks at Big Cedar Lodge. Wide fairways and big greens by intent — it was built for resort golfers, not to defend par. The thing everyone remembers is the extra hole afterwards: a par 3 played down into a limestone sinkhole with a waterfall behind the green, designed by Johnny Morris rather than Woods, and not counted on the card.
descriptions.Poppy Ridge: The Northern California Golf Association commissioned Rees Jones, then Golf Digest's architect of the year, to put 27 holes into the hills above Livermore, and Poppy Ridge opened to public play in 1996 as three nines named Chardonnay, Merlot and Zinfandel. That is no longer what stands. Jay Blasi rebuilt the property into a single eighteen, which opened in May 2025, with a par-34 nine beside it made up mostly of holes kept from the old Merlot.
descriptions.Red Tail Run: A Raymond Floyd signature course built by the Decatur Park District on the south side of town, which opened for play on 25 April 2006. The park district's announcement called it the fourth signature public course in Illinois. Par 72 over 6,915 yards, municipal, and a good deal more ambitious than a city usually attempts, which is most of the reason anyone outside central Illinois has heard of it.
descriptions.Revelstoke: The land was set aside as a park in 1898, and from 1908 the Revelstoke Turf Association raced horses over what is now the back nine. The first nine holes of golf came in 1924, and the clubhouse is the agricultural hall built in 1912 for the fall fair, its cupola having served as the race caller's booth. Norman Woods took the course to eighteen holes in 1974. The Labour Day tournament here is said to be the longest-running amateur event in British Columbia.
descriptions.Samoset: Golf started here as nine holes in 1902; Robert Elder rebuilt it as eighteen in 1974, and the Maine architect Bradley Booth reworked the 4th, 5th, 14th and 18th and added the practice ground in 2000. The 4th plays along the bay and now has a stone seawall wrapped around a contoured green. For much of the seaward stretch a granite wall is all that stands between the golf and the Atlantic. Par 70 over 6,081 yards.
descriptions.Sand Valley: Coore and Crenshaw's course opened in 2017, the fifth they had built for Mike Keiser and the first of them nowhere near an ocean. The site is a thousand acres of dunes left in central Wisconsin by the retreating ice, carrying scrub oak, heather, bearberry and blueberry off the line of play. It runs about 6,900 yards. Four more courses have since gone in around it, including a seventeen-hole par 3.
descriptions.South Cape Owner's Club: Kyle Phillips built it in 2013 for the Korean fashion designer Jae Bong Chung, on cliffs at the southern end of the peninsula near Namhae, with the sea in view from all eighteen holes. The stretch the designers call the promenade to the sea begins at the downhill par-5 11th and runs through to the par-3 16th; beside the 15th green sits a sharp triangular mound of turf that reviewers never fail to mention. It plays 6,685 metres from the back.
descriptions.Stonecutters Ridge: Bob Harrison, then running Greg Norman's Australian design office, did the original routing over varied ground at Colebee, on what had been a chicken farm and is now a 160-hectare housing development. Construction began in 2008, stalled with the Sydney property market, and was finished by Norman's Florida team after the Australian office closed. The course opened in 2012, Norman's first in Sydney.
descriptions.Stonewolf: Jack Nicklaus laid it out with Bruce Borland and it opened in 1997 as a daily-fee course in the Illinois suburbs east of St Louis, one of only four Nicklaus designs in Illinois and Missouri and one of the few anywhere that anybody can simply book. It plays 6,943 yards from the back with five sets of tees, rated between about 73.5 and 74.0 depending on the source, with a slope in the high 130s to mid 140s.
descriptions.Teton Pines: Arnold Palmer and Ed Seay turned ranch land at Wilson, just outside Jackson, into a course that opened in 1987, and Golf Digest called the resort the third-best new golf resort in the country that year. It sits at about 6,200 feet on the flat of the valley, with the Grand Teton range filling the view rather than the course being cut into it. Par 72, slope 137 from the back tees, and green-fee play is taken as well as members.
descriptions.The Federal Club: Arnold Palmer and Ed Seay's course north of Richmond, with Harrison Minchew's firm also credited, opened in 2007 inside a residential development and was specified bentgrass from tee to green. It did not last in that form: the club went bankrupt in 2010. It was reconstituted as a private club afterwards and has since been reported profitable with 344 members, which is a more eventful history than most suburban Virginia golf can offer.
descriptions.The Golf Club at Black Rock: Jim Engh's course opened in 2003 near Lake Coeur d'Alene and won best new private club that year; in 2009 it became the first course in Idaho to reach Golf Digest's top 100. None of the holes are actually on the lake. What it has instead is outcrops of black basalt, wetland, prairie and woodland in quick succession, which is where the rock and the name come from. Members and their guests only.
descriptions.The Hills: Michael Hill, the jeweller, asked his friend John Darby for a putting green on a former deer farm outside Arrowtown; the thing grew a hole at a time until Darby had laid out a full course. It held the New Zealand Open for the first time in 2007 and has shared the championship with Millbrook since. Large sculpture is part of the place: a five-metre weta on the 1st fairway, dragonflies set into the water at Dragonfly Lake, a three-metre walking woman on a bridge at the 4th.
descriptions.The Idaho Club: Jack Nicklaus's 2008 course lies about eight miles east of Sandpoint in the Pack River valley, on ground that had been the Hidden Lakes course, and it is the only eighteen-hole Nicklaus Signature layout in Idaho. Water figures on nine holes. Its recent history has been financial rather than architectural: the development failed, and Valiant Idaho took the property over and reopened the golf in 2017 with a new 7,500 square foot clubhouse.
descriptions.The National (Old): Robert Trent Jones Jr got the job after Pete Dye declined to fly to Australia to see the site, and the course opened in 1988 as the club's first. Unlike the Moonah and Gunnamatta courses beside it, it is laid out in woodland rather than open links ground, over 6,313 metres of hilly Cape Schanck. Australian Golf Digest has ranked it 87th in the world. Long Island Country Club merged into the club after a members' vote in 2014.
descriptions.The Oconee at Lake Reynolds: Rees Jones designed it with Greg Muirhead and it joined his portfolio in 2002, routed to use the fall of the land down to the shoreline at Greensboro. Lake water, creeks and ponds are in play on nine holes, including each of the last four. It held the PGA Cup in 2007. Reviewers tend to find the earlier holes straightforward and the closing lakeside stretch the reason to come.
descriptions.The Prestwick (Indiana): A Bob Simmons course in Avon, west of Indianapolis, opened in 1974 and playing 6,885 yards to a par of 72, rated 73.7 with a slope of 127. It takes green-fee play as well as members, which is not what the name implies. There is a second Prestwick in Indiana, at Frankfort, laid out by Larry Packard in 1964, and the two are regularly confused in course directories.
descriptions.The Reserve at Moonlight Basin: Jack Nicklaus's course at Big Sky sits near 7,500 feet, which is why the card reads as it does. The first nine holes were built in 2008 and the full eighteen opened in August 2015. The 17th is a par 5 of 777 yards, among the longest holes in the game. In July 2020 the course staged the televised Match, Phil Mickelson and Tom Brady against Bryson DeChambeau and Aaron Rodgers, which is how most people have seen it.
descriptions.The Sanctuary: Jim Engh designed it for Dave Liniger, co-founder of RE/MAX, and it opened in 1997 south-west of Denver, built by Niebur Golf of Colorado Springs. It has never taken public play. The Linigers open it for charity tournaments and selected groups, usually at a donation well over $1,500 a head, and the club's own figures put cumulative net proceeds since 1997 at more than $73 million. Few private courses anywhere can show a number like that.
descriptions.The Wilds: Tom Weiskopf and Jay Morrish laid it out south-west of Minneapolis and it opened in 1995: 7,025 yards, par 72, with about 150 feet of elevation change and water in play on nearly half the holes. The slope of 140 from the back is stiff for a public course in Minnesota, with the rating around 74.5. Golf Digest has rated it four stars.
descriptions.Tiburon (Great White / Hammerhead): Greg Norman's Naples course, laid out through cypress and pine with coquina shell waste areas instead of rough — you can ground your club, but you cannot predict the lie. It hosts the QBE Shootout each December and the LPGA's season finale. Flat Florida ground made interesting by sand rather than by earth-moving.
descriptions.Ute Creek: The City of Longmont approved the site plan in 1995 and the course, by the Robert Trent Jones II group, opened in 1997. It is still municipal, run by the city, and stretches from 5,509 to 7,167 yards at a par of 72, which is a great deal of golf for a city to keep up on the plains north of Denver. The front range provides the backdrop and the altitude does the rest.
descriptions.Victoria National: Tom Fazio routed it between the spoil mounds and flooded pits of Peabody Coal's Victoria mine, worked from the 1950s until 1977, about seven miles east of Evansville; it opened in 1998. The Friedman family developed it and sold in 2010, and the Dormie Network bought it in 2018. The Korn Ferry Tour has played here since 2012 and the course now holds the season-ending Tour Championship, which is where most people have seen those black water hazards.
descriptions.Waterlefe: Ted McAnlis's course opened in 2000 as the centrepiece of a residential community of about 175 acres off I-75 east of Bradenton, running down towards the river. Water figures on close to every hole, as hazard or as scenery, along with the alligators, turtles and occasional otter that come with it. It has been used for U.S. Open local qualifying at least six times since 2002, which is a better recommendation than most Florida community courses can claim.
descriptions.Whisper Rock (Upper): The Upper is Tom Fazio's course at Whisper Rock, opened in 2005. The Lower, four years older, is the Mickelson one, co-designed with the Dallas architect Gary Stephenson for the club's owner Gregg Tryhus. The Upper's name comes from the 12th through the 16th, where the holes climb briefly into higher rocky ground. The club bills the pair as the Pine Valley of the Southwest, and the membership in north Scottsdale is heavy with tour players.
descriptions.Wynn Golf Club: Tom Fazio built the original course behind the hotel and returned with his son Logan to rebuild it after a two-year closure; it reopened on 11 October 2019 with eight entirely new holes and ten reworked ones on 129 acres. More than 400,000 cubic yards of earth and three hundred trees were moved to widen the landing areas and change the elevations. The 18th became a par 3 that can be stretched to 249 yards, its green set in front of a waterfall 35 feet high and 100 feet wide.
descriptions.US Top 18: A composite round: famous American holes lifted off their home courses and stitched into one eighteen. Nothing here is a real place, which is the point, because the interest is in recognising each hole as it arrives. A simulator-only build, and an easy introduction for somebody who has only ever seen these holes on television.
descriptions.Spa-Francorchamps: Eighteen holes laid over the Formula One circuit in the Belgian Ardennes, Eau Rouge included. A simulator-only build, and the curiosity is in how a racing circuit reads as golf: long sweeping corridors and gradients that were cut for cars, including a climb no golf architect would ever have drawn.
descriptions.Isla Nublar Golf Club: Jurassic Park as a golf course. Par 70 at 6,645 yards, built at full length rather than as a novelty, so the dinosaurs are scenery around a real routing instead of the whole of the entertainment. Simulator only, and the companion to the par-3 version of the same island.
descriptions.Stonehenge: Golf around the stone circle on Salisbury Plain, which no planning authority on earth would permit and which is the reason the build exists. Mountain terrain, par 72, 6,732 yards, simulator only. The one course in the catalogue whose central piece of scenery needs no explaining to anybody.
descriptions.The Ancient Course: The name is bait. This is not St Andrews but St. Andromeda, on Mars: a links routing transplanted to another planet, which is the whole of the joke. A simulator-only build, worth loading for the gap between what the title promises and what arrives on the screen.
descriptions.Ashen Cliffs: An invented volcanic coast with a links routing laid on top of it. The builder asks for gusty wind and hard ground, which is the condition the holes were drawn for, so playing it soft and still misses the intention. Par 71 at 6,808 yards, simulator only.
descriptions.Bushwood CC: Bushwood Country Club, the club from Caddyshack, built as a parkland course rather than as a gag: par 71 at 6,710 yards. Simulator only. The film is the reason anybody loads it, and the fact that the golf underneath stands up on its own is the better part of the bargain.
descriptions.Canyon Run (Champions): The full-length companion to the Canyon Run par 3, by the same builder and on the same invented desert ground. Par 72. The short course is the better known of the two; this is the one for when the par 3 has been played out and the same country is wanted at full size.
descriptions.Central Park North: Eighteen holes routed through Central Park, which amounts to golf through Manhattan with the skyline on every horizon. 7,721 yards, simulator only, and long enough that the premise is not doing all the work. The northern half of a pair.
descriptions.Central Park South: The other half of the Manhattan build, 7,384 yards through the southern end of the park. The same premise and the same reason to play it: a city used as scenery for a round nobody could ever stage there. Simulator only, and the two are meant to go together.
descriptions.Clarkson's Farm: Diddly Squat, the Oxfordshire farm from Jeremy Clarkson's television series, rendered as something golf-adjacent. Not really a course: it is a target range with animals to aim at, best loaded in On Course Practice mode and treated as an hour of hitting at things rather than a round with a card.
descriptions.Course of the Dead: A horror build, and a long one at 7,515 yards, so it is a real round rather than a walk through a haunted house. The premise is in the title and the scenery carries it; underneath sits a standard parkland par 72. Simulator only, and it belongs in October.
descriptions.Gilded Dunes: Invented desert golf with the money turned up, in the Dubai idiom. Firm and fast across 7,171 yards, so the ball runs a long way and the trouble is sand rather than water. Simulator only, and listed among the kinder rounds here despite the yardage.
descriptions.GSPro Ballpark: Three holes inside a baseball stadium, 562 yards in total. Not a course and not pretending to be one: a twenty-minute curiosity that exists because a simulator has no groundsman to answer to. Worth one loop to see the stadium, and little reason to go back.
descriptions.Halo: Golf on the ringworld from Halo, the video game, with a coastal routing laid along the inside of an enormous artificial ring. Par 72 at 6,921 yards, simulator only. The setting is the reason to load it and the architecture underneath is conventional enough to keep a card on.
descriptions.Middle Earth: Tolkien, at length. Number two on GSPro's 2025 Wrapped and the most elaborate of the fantasy builds, which in practice means the landscape was the project and the golf was fitted into it. Mountain ground, par 73, 6,480 yards. Simulator only, and the one to show anybody who doubts what these builds can look like.
descriptions.Mos Desertly: Star Wars on Tatooine, by the builder of Sanctuary Moon, with the name doing the joke unassisted. Desert golf, par 69 at 6,758 yards, so shorter and tighter than its Endor counterpart. Simulator only, and the pair are meant to be played back to back.
